findings.title: The NCAA Rule 7 scoring engine is fully built, sourced, tested - and wired to nothing
evidence: packages/core/src/lib/ncaaScoringRules.ts is 1401 lines: 14 meet formats, exhibition isolation (7-10-1), DQ place advancement (7-7), tie division (7-8), lost-place accounting, per-format maxScorersPerTeam.
tests/ncaaScoringRules.test.ts is 864 lines.
grep across the monorepo for every export returns exactly two consumers: its own test file and a re-export in packages/core/src/index.ts. Zero product code calls it.

The product scores via calculatePoints in packages/core/src/lib/utils.ts against the legacy ScoringSettings shape (consumers: scoringEngine, rosterOptimizer, arbitrage/*, scenarioDiff, matrix swimCloudMeetImportBridge).

Provenance verified this session: data/scoring_rules/sources/ncaascoring.pdf sha256 5b98f8f69470606ea179b053b86d7fb4451f61a874c0fff5d8d18b369d6bb92e is byte-identical to a fresh fetch of https://meets.swimdna.org/media/ncaascoring.pdf and matches the manifest.
findings.consequence: ScoringSettings models relay points as a scalar relayMultiplier. That is exactly correct for all six championship field sizes (relay table is 2x individual at 6/8/12/16/18/24 - all verified against the rulebook). It is structurally WRONG for every non-championship format: dual 6+ lanes is individual 9-4-3-2-1 with relays 11-4-2 (11 is not 2x9); dual <=5 lanes is 5-3-1 with relays 7 (7 is not 2x5). The three dual diving tables (7-1-4) are also inexpressible - diving is modelled only as diverScorerWeight, not as its own place-value table. A dual meet is the most common format in college swimming and the app cannot represent one today.

findings.title: Crawl resume is per-capture; the global page store is not consulted across meets
evidence: data/swimcloud-captures/pages/ is keyed GLOBALLY by canonicalUrl (123 files on disk), so page bytes are already shared across captures.

But crawler-content.ts readAlreadyCaptured() builds its skip set from a single SUBJECT's capture record (GET /api/swimcloud/captures/{id}), not from the global page store. A different meet re-fetches pages whose bytes are already on disk.
Page-kind breakdown of the real 234-page capture: swimmerTimes 184 (78.6%), meetTeamSwims 42 (17.9%), teamRoster 8 (3.4%).
A swimmer's personal-bests page is the SAME canonicalUrl regardless of which meet is being crawled, so it is the page kind that repeats most across a season's crawls.
Measured wall time: meetTeamSwims 42 pages/122s (2981ms gap), teamRoster 8 pages/21s (3002ms gap), swimmerTimes 184 pages/75s (409ms gap, pooled). Total ~218s for 4 teams.
findings.consequence: Two real speedups remain available WITHOUT touching the 3000ms floor the user ruled out (d3): (1) Job-scoped page selection - swimmerTimes is 78.6% of all pages fetched, and a meet-results-only job does not need any of them. (2) Cross-capture reuse - consult the global pages/ store when building the skip set, gated by a real freshness policy, since a personal-bests page legitimately changes as a swimmer races. The existing provisional/final cacheStatus is the right mechanism: a finished meet's pages are immutable and can be promoted to 'final'; provisional pages need a TTL. Both reduce traffic rather than increasing it.
findings.correctionNote: An earlier reading of this finding in the same session was WRONG and was corrected before any work was briefed on it. The wrong version said 'every page is provisional, so a re-crawl re-fetches everything'. That is false: extensions/swimcloud-companion/src/captureResume.ts implements a real, unit-tested, fail-safe resume, and re-crawling the SAME meet correctly skips pages already stored. The cacheStatus field belongs to the server-side Track B Playwright cache (packages/swimcloud/src/cache.ts), not to the extension's resume path. Recorded here so nobody re-derives the wrong conclusion from the raw cacheStatus counts.

findings.title: RESOLVED ALREADY - prelims/finals rounds are resolved from meetEvent pages
evidence: packages/matrix/src/lib/swimCloudMeetImportBridge.ts resolves a swim's round from /results/{meetId}/event/{n}/ pages, which print one caption-labelled table per round plus the real meet Score column. Its own comment: 'This is what turns "excluded as ambiguous" into "scored as the round it actually was".'

The eventResults option is genuinely supplied, not an optional-and-never-passed parameter: apps/shell/lib/swimcloudCaptureRoutes.ts parses them (line ~713/735) and packages/matrix/src/components/OpsModule.tsx:485 passes selection.eventResults into the bridge.

The crawl actually fetches them: crawler-content.ts runs runEventResultsPass (line ~922), planned by planEventResultsSteps -> planMeetEventResults, pooled at EVENT_RESULTS_CONCURRENCY=3 / EVENT_RESULTS_STAGGER_MS=400.

Exclusion via 'ambiguous-round-duplicate' still exists as the correct fallback for a swim whose event page is absent, did not parse, or carried no round caption - absence of data, never a guess. That is right and stays.
findings.consequence: The better a swimmer is, the more likely they vanish from an opponent-scouting import. Directly undermines user decision d1's scouting/projection requirement. Candidate fix: use meetEvent pages, which do carry round context, as a disambiguation SOURCE (not a guess).
findings.correctionNote: An earlier reading of this finding in the same session was WRONG. It was taken from plans/2026-09-10/01-SWIMCLOUD-SCORING-CORRECTNESS.md, which describes the problem and an interim fix that EXCLUDED ambiguous prelims/finals groups wholesale. A later change resolved it properly and the plan doc was never updated. Do not re-open this from that doc. Lesson recorded: verify a plan doc's claim against the code before briefing work on it - this repo's docs lag its code.
findings.consequenceForP3: Important knock-on for the crawl-speed work: the archived 234-page capture (2026-09-10) PREDATES the event-results pass and contains zero meetEvent pages. A crawl run today therefore fetches MORE pages than that sample - one meetEvent page per distinct event on top of the 234. The user's 'data pulling is very slow' impression is likely of a post-eventResults crawl, so the real current page count is higher than the measured baseline. Re-measure against a current crawl before claiming any speedup percentage.

findings.title: Workspace backup works but is unreachable and never automatic
evidence: POST /api/workspaces/backup exists (apps/shell/server.ts:570) and repo.backup() is implemented correctly for both SqliteRepo and PgRepo - it calls writeJsonBackup(exportAll()), reading THROUGH the database rather than copying files, so it is write-ahead-log safe.
That route has exactly one caller: itself. grep across packages/ and apps/ for 'workspaces/backup' returns no UI call site. A coach cannot back up from inside the app.
Nothing schedules a backup. repo.backup() is never invoked on startup, before an import, before an optimizer apply, or before a delete.
data/backups/ holds exactly 4 files, all from 2026-09-08, and they are raw .db/.db-shm/.db-wal copies - made by a script, not by this route.

Live state today: data/omniswim.db is 4096 bytes while data/omniswim.db-wal is 3.5MB. Anything that naively copied only the .db file would capture an almost-empty database. The implemented backup does not have this bug; a hand-rolled one would.
findings.consequence: The user's stated goal is a suite 'ready to be properly used in an actual setting'. Losing a roster the night before a meet is the worst realistic failure this app has, and today nothing prevents it. The mechanism already exists and is correct - it just has no trigger and no button. This is a small amount of work for a large amount of safety.

findings.title: Button adoption is low because the primitive cannot express the app's prevailing button style, not because nobody tried
evidence: packages/ui/src/components/Button.tsx line 46 bakes 'font-bold' and 'disabled:opacity-50' into the BASE class, applied to every variant and size, with no prop to vary either.
Sizes fix the radius too: sm=rounded-lg + text-ui-micro, md=rounded-xl + text-ui-label, lg=rounded-2xl + text-ui-body.

The real call sites in packages/manager use combinations the primitive has no way to produce - e.g. rounded-lg + font-medium + disabled:opacity-40, or rounded-lg + font-semibold + disabled:opacity-60.

P4 (worker) audited all 28 raw <button> elements across the six files it touched and converted ZERO, because every conversion would have visibly changed corner radius, font weight, or disabled opacity - and the brief's bar was zero visual change. Its per-file reasoning is in the P4 agent report.
Adoption today: Button imported by 4 of 55 files; 122 raw <button> vs 9 <Button>.
findings.consequence: The 2026-09-10 diagnosis framed low Button adoption as a discipline problem. It is a fit problem: the primitive is more opinionated than the app it serves. Converging on it requires a DECISION first - either relax Button (make weight, radius and disabled opacity variant-controlled) or restyle the app to Button's look (a real, visible change needing sign-off). Doing a mass conversion without that decision would silently restyle ~120 controls.
findings.status: CLOSED 2026-09-21 - app restyled onto Button (commit db298ad0)
findings.userDecision: Restyle the app to Button, not relax Button. The visual change is accepted: corners rounder, labels bolder, disabled states lighter. Dispatched to a worker covering 167 raw <button> elements across manager (111), ui (22), apps/shell (21), metrics (20) and matrix (13). Tab strips and SegmentedControl are excluded - they are a navigation idiom with an active-underline affordance Button cannot express.
findings.result: Raw <button> 187 -> 44; <Button> usages 30 -> 173. 143 controls converted. Verified with the Playwright e2e suite, which clicks these controls for real: 963 unit tests, 84 script tests, lint clean on all three gates, production build green. No behaviour changed and no test selector needed touching.
deliberatelyLeftRaw: Tab strips (nav-tab-*) and WizardShell's ARIA tablist - a navigation idiom with an active-underline affordance Button cannot express.
Disclosure headers and full-width row selectors - laid out by their container rather than styled as controls.
VideoPlayerParts transport bar - deliberately overrides theme colours for legibility over footage.
Menu's trigger - its className prop REPLACES rather than merges, so wrapping it would change that contract for every caller.
Toast's close button - a bespoke CSS class that would fight Button's utilities at equal specificity.
findings.primitiveFindings: cn() uses tailwind-merge, so className reliably overrides Button's own display/padding/rounding utilities - conversions were more tractable than expected. Four variants and three sizes covered every genuine action button, so the primitive did NOT need widening. Its real gaps are narrow: no way to express a replace-not-merge className contract, a bespoke equal-specificity CSS class, or a theme-invariant control.

findings.title: Selecting the invitational scoring preset crashed with an unhandled promise rejection
evidence: packages/core/src/lib/scoringPresets.ts:113 rethrows HostPublishedTableRequiredError for a format the NCAA publishes no table for (Rule 7-4 leaves it to the host).

findings.title: RESOLVED - the swimmer-times page builds its table in the browser, so a fetched copy never contains it
evidence: Verified independently against data/swimcloud-captures/captures/meet-356467.json, not taken from the agent's report.
swimmerTimes: 73 pages HTTP 200, 111 pages HTTP 429 (rate-limited, no bytes stored). Outcomes: ok/200 x73, http-error/429 x111.

The 73 that DID return 200 contain no <table> - the parser fails loudly on all 184 ('a swimmer times page is expected to contain the Personal Bests table'). So the entire pass produced nothing usable.
By contrast meetTeamSwims (42 pages) and teamRoster (8 pages) were 200 across the board - a 100% success rate.
The difference is pacing. The two clean passes run SEQUENTIALLY at the 3000ms MIN_DELAY_MS floor. The failing pass is the one deliberate relaxation: SWIMMER_TIMES_CONCURRENCY=3 with a 400ms stagger.
findings.consequence: This reframes the user's 'data pulling is very slow' complaint. The pass that was made fast is being throttled and mostly failing, so 78.6% of that crawl's traffic bought nothing. Slowing the swimmer-times pool would likely make it FASTER in effective terms - fewer 429s, fewer wasted requests, actual data returned. That points the OPPOSITE way from relaxing pacing, so it does not conflict with user decision d3. Note boundedFetchPool.ts's own header already called this risk: 'Running two or three swimmer-times fetches at once is a materially different traffic pattern from a single sequential stream, and it is more likely - not less - to be noticed by request-pattern fingerprinting.' That prediction appears to have come true and nobody measured it until now.
openQuestions: Does the 429 clear with sequential pacing? Needs a real, human-present test against the live site.
Why do the 73 successful fetches carry no table? Possibly a soft-block/challenge page rather than the real page, or a page-shape change. Worth parsing one stored body to see what actually came back.
findings.rootCause: NOT rate limiting, which was the initial hypothesis. All 73 successfully-fetched bodies in the archived capture are complete documents (end </html>), 15-17KB, contain ZERO <table> elements, and load /media/webpack/swimmerProfileTimes/index.*.js. They render only the shell: nav, swimmer name and school, and the Home/Meets/Times/Rankings tab strip. By contrast 10 of 10 sampled meetTeamSwims bodies from the same crawl DO contain their tables - those pages are server-rendered. So pacing was never the issue: a crawl with zero 429s would still parse zero rows.
findings.whyTheCodebaseBelievedOtherwise: parser.ts asserted the Personal Bests table was 'fully server-rendered (no click needed)', citing a real 2026-09-09 capture. That capture is tests/fixtures/swimcloud-real-swimmer-times-1472365.html, whose own header records it was taken 'via the browser extension (Track A, clipboard)' - which copies the RENDERED DOM after the page's JavaScript has run. It is evidence the table exists on screen and says nothing about what the server sends. That single wrong inference justified a fetch-based pass that could never parse a row. The comment is now corrected.
findings.fix: SWIMCLOUD_DOM_RENDERED_PASSES in crawlPlan.ts records the pass as unfetchable, with the evidence. planScopedMeetCrawl declines it and REPORTS the decline (declinedNeedingRenderedDom) rather than dropping it silently, because a coach who picked a season-bests scope must be told why none arrived. The crawler panel explains the cause and points at the clipboard path, which works because it reads the rendered DOM. 2 mutations proven.
findings.remainingOpenQuestion: The 111 HTTP 429s are real and unexplained, but now moot for this pass since it no longer runs. If a future pass is added over swimmer pages, the 429 rate should be re-measured first.

findings.title: ManagerApp called a hook after an early return - a reachable React crash

The EmptyState rendered by that early return has a 'New workspace' button, so activeWorkspace goes absent -> present on the SAME mounted component and the next render calls more hooks than the previous one. Deleting the last workspace does it in reverse.

findings.consequence: Fixed by splitting the guard into a wrapper component so every hook below it runs unconditionally. This is the finding that justified adding ESLint on its own.

findings.title: Time trials double-count against the entry cap: 8 of 13 over-limit warnings on real data are false
evidence: REPRODUCED INDEPENDENTLY against data/meets.json, workspace Blank Workspace 1 (NSISC, maxTotalEntriesPerSwimmer 7).

Oskar Cebula has 8 rows including BOTH 'Event 26 Men 100 Yard Breaststroke' AND 'Event 100 Men 100 Yard Breaststroke Time Trial'. The same 100 Breaststroke counts twice: 8/7 flagged, 7/7 once the time trial is excluded.

Across the real meet: 13 athletes flagged over the cap, 8 of them false once time trials are excluded. Men 1 (Cebula). Women 7 (Cleasant, Shipp, Mikayla Kloth, Hite, Murphy, Tankersley, Jordon Kloth). The other 5 are genuinely over: real data, not a counting bug.
Roughly 62% of the compliance warnings a coach sees on this meet are wrong.
The rows already carry isTimeTrial true. The data distinguishes them; the counting does not look.

Root cause: entryCapKey (packages/core/src/lib/swimmerEntryLimits.ts:94) keys on the raw HyTek event string, which is docs/INVARIANTS.md item 3. It collapses prelims/finals only because HyTek repeats the identical label; a time trial gets a new event number and a Time Trial suffix, so it never collapses.
The same count gates canAcceptAnotherEntry, so an affected swimmer is also blocked from adding a legitimate entry.

Everywhere else treats a time trial as outside the program: canonicalProgramEvent returns null for them, buildMeetEventLabelIndex skips them, computeVisibleEvents hides them, and they score 0. Entry counting is the one place that does not.
findings.whyNotFixed: Whether a time trial counts against a 7-event entry limit is a competition-rules question. CLAUDE.md forbids inventing one, and a test written now would pin whichever answer was guessed.
optionsForUser: (a) Skip isTimeTrial rows in countSwimmerEntries. Matches how the rest of the codebase models time trials. Simplest.

(b) Key entryCapKey through canonicalProgramEvent so one program event is one entry however it was labelled. Narrower: a time trial of an event the swimmer did not otherwise enter would still cost an entry.
(c) Leave as is, if NSISC really does count a time trial against the 7.
findings.userRuling: Time trials do NOT count against a swimmer's entry limit.
findings.implementation: countSwimmerEntries skips rows with isTimeTrial. Chosen over keying entryCapKey through canonicalProgramEvent, because that narrower fix would still charge an entry for a time trial of an event the swimmer did not otherwise swim, and the ruling is that a time trial never costs one. Verified through the real function against data/meets.json: Oskar Cebula now counts 7 of 7, not 8 of 7. Guarded by scripts/test_entry_limits_time_trials.mjs (6 cases, registered), with two mutations proven and the under-count case checked in isolation because it would otherwise die on an earlier assertion.

findings.title: The scoring safety net leans on scripts/, which vitest does not see
evidence: A 12-mutation sweep: 11 caught. Four scoring mutations were each caught by exactly one check, and in three cases that check was a scripts/ test invisible to npx vitest run: entryCapKey collapse, alias-resolved override keys, deriveAutoScorerKeys genderFilter, and buildMeetEventLabelIndex skipping time trials.
All four passed under a full vitest run.

aFinalBracket's Math.floor(len/2) fallback is unreachable: all 21 built-in presets carrying settings define aFinalBracketSize, and mergeScoringSettings always spreads DEFAULT_SCORING_SETTINGS, which sets 8. Mutating the fallback survived everything; mutating the reachable half was caught loudly by test_nsisc_team_totals.
findings.consequence: An unregistered script in scripts/ is a hole in the primary guard of the scoring path, not a tidiness issue. That is why f16's registration guard matters structurally. The unreachable aFinalBracket fallback is flagged because a future preset omitting the field would silently take an untested path.

findings.title: computeVacateRelayLegNames builds its lookup before the alias collapse
evidence: packages/core/src/lib/rosterLineupAudit.ts:174 uses the identity resolver; whatIfProjection.ts:400 calls it before aliases are collapsed.
An override recorded under the canonical spelling cannot match a relay leg carrying an alias spelling, so a swimmer toggled off as a scorer would keep their relay leg in the what-if projection.
NOT REPRODUCED against today's data: Blank Workspace 1 happens to carry overrides under both spellings for all three aliased athletes, and every relay leg uses the canonical one.
findings.consequence: Latent identity mismatch of the exact class INVARIANTS item 6 describes. A new alias would expose it.
findings.status: CLOSED 2026-09-21 - reproduced, fixed and mutation-proven (commit f83173af)
findings.reproduction: Built the case the hunt could not: four relay LEG rows (a row whose name equals its team is the aggregate entry and is skipped by the audit, so a team-named fixture produces no relay template at all), the first leg printed under an alias spelling, and a scorerRosterOverride filed under the canonical spelling marking that swimmer a non-scorer. Without a resolver the leg is not vacated; with one it is.
findings.fix: computeVacateRelayLegNames takes an optional resolver and passes it to buildScorerRosterLookup; whatIfProjection builds one from the workspace and passes it down. Existing callers that omit it keep the identity default, so nothing else changed.
findings.testingNote: The first version of the guard asserted only that SOMETHING was vacated. It stayed green under the mutation, because the other three legs are non-scorers regardless. Caught by mutation before it was trusted; the guard now names the swimmer and carries a control case pinning the identity default.

openDecisions.question: How aggressive should automatic backups be?
openDecisions.options: On server start only (cheapest, one per session) / start + before each destructive operation (safest, more files) / plus a periodic timer while running.
openDecisions.recommendation: Start + before destructive operations, with retention capped at N most recent. A backup is a JSON export of all workspaces; the current meets.json is 3MB, so retention matters.

openDecisions.question: Is data/meets.json a curated demo seed, or a snapshot of live working state? Today it is both.
openDecisions.context: docs/INVARIANTS.md item 1: data/meets.json is gitignored BUT tracked, and SqliteRepo.init() seeds data/omniswim.db from it on a fresh checkout. It currently holds the real HSU/OBU workspaces - 3MB, 871-1029 athlete-history rows each. Anyone who clones this repo boots into the user's actual roster data. Carried over from plans/STATE.md's own open question 5, still unanswered.
openDecisions.whyItMatters: Only matters if anyone but the user ever runs this. If the app stays single-user it is a non-issue and the seed is a feature. If a second coach ever uses it, they should boot into an empty or demo workspace, not someone else's roster.
openDecisions.answer: User: 'currently its a personal/my coach's tool but we will make this a tool that should be shareable later on when i am confident in releasing this.' So: TWO users today (the user and their coach), not one. The seed data is acceptable now and is NOT a deadline blocker. It becomes a RELEASE BLOCKER: before any public/shared release, data/meets.json must stop being both the live working store and the fresh-install seed. A new installation must boot into an empty or curated demo workspace, never into a real team's roster. Record this in the P6 guide's release-readiness section.
openDecisions.resolution: data/meets.json is untracked and local; a fresh install seeds from the committed data/demo-seed.json - 29KB, two invented schools, sixteen invented swimmers, workspace named 'Demo meet (sample data - not real results)'. Workspace ids regenerate per install. An unreadable seed degrades to a blank workspace. Existing installs unaffected: SqliteRepo still migrates from a local meets.json, verified by booting the real data dir and seeing all three workspaces. DATA_DIR now takes an OMNI_DATA_DIR override, which is how the fresh-install path was tested without touching real data. tests/demoSeed.test.ts (7 cases, 2 mutations) fails if meets.json is ever tracked again, if the seed grows past 200KB, if its name stops declaring itself a sample, or if any name or team in it appears in the live store. INVARIANTS item 1 rewritten - it documented the behaviour this removes.
openDecisions.residualRisk: The repository HISTORY still contains the old meets.json. New clones no longer receive it as data, but it is readable in past commits and the repo is public. Removing it requires rewriting history, which is destructive and was not done unilaterally. Flagged to the user.
